items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: And comes down into people like Chet Baker and eventually the Miles Davises and, in other words, I see three distinct lines of development.

ctx.x: That worked certainly. Let's see. We were talking about recording sessions. It was Joe Maera- Mm-hm. He worked with him. Were you working for Joe Maera- Mm-hm.

Not really. What was the basis? No. Let me see what would I say was the basis. Joe, as you know, was very much interested in getting the music of New Orleans recorded. recorded. He has a feeling of commitment about it, the fact that there are a lot of musicians who hadn't been recorded or hadn't been recorded properly. And of course I felt the same way about it, and I always thought of myself as helping out, you know, in many cases proposing and producing sessions myself that I thought were suitable. And so there…
Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: Wouldn't he have been closer to a more melodic lyrical player, like maybe Chet Baker?

ctx.x: I think he would have gravitated to that and possibly contributed to making some kind of sense out of it. I believe that he would have played bop during the period when it was popular. But I believe that he would have eventually drifted off into some non-objective area, which would have been of the Coltrane persuasion, rather than in any real organized way.
Wouldn't he have been closer to a more melodic lyrical player, like maybe Chet Baker?

Well, except for the fact that I believe that the lack of acceptance of that kind of music would have proven to be very discouraging to him. I believe that he would have been considered to be old hat and no longer of interest. I don't think that he would have survived as a favorite among the musicians. And I really do believe that that was necessary to him. I believe that he had to have sounding boards and he had to have... Okay. Okay, the third reel is on. Good.
